opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't an easy decision. The big labs have incredible resources: huge compute budgets, very strong teams, and products that reach hundreds of millions of people. I respect that a lot, and I had good conversations with several of them.

But after many years in large organizations, I started asking what problem I most wanted to spend the next few years on. For me, that problem is how AI systems can improve themselves: how a model can discover better reasoning strategies, better training signals, maybe even better versions of itself, instead of relying only on humans to hand-design every step. I think that is one of the most important open questions in the field right now.

At a big company, even a very good one, much of the energy naturally goes into the main product line, the next flagship model, and the competitive race. That's understandable, but it means more exploratory, long-horizon ideas can struggle to get attention. At RSI, the whole team is focused on that one direction. We can move fast, try unconventional approaches, and if something doesn't work, change course the next week without going through layers of planning.

There's also a personal side. I've always enjoyed being close to the actual research: writing code, looking at experiments, arguing about ideas with a small group of people. In a smaller setting I get to do more of that, rather than mainly managing roadmaps.

So it came down to focus and freedom. The large labs will do many important things, but I felt the specific bet I care about most had a better chance of being explored seriously in a place built around it from day one.

r003.rationale: It says RSI can change course quickly, but does not identify communication at large AI companies as too slow to keep pace with AI development.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it came down to what I actually wanted to spend the next several years of my life doing, rather than which logo I wanted on my badge.

When I talked to the big labs, the conversations were very polished, but they were mostly about slotting me into an existing roadmap. There's a train already moving, it's enormous, and the question is which car you'd like to sit in. That's a perfectly good career, and I have a lot of respect for the people doing it. But I've already spent a long time inside big organizations, and I know what the day-to-day looks like. A lot of your energy goes into coordination, into alignment meetings, into defending a direction before you've even had the chance to test it.

What drew me to RSI was that the central question is still open. We're trying to understand whether a system can genuinely improve its own capabilities in a sustained, measurable way, and nobody has a clean answer to that yet. That's the kind of problem I've always cared about, going back to my work on reasoning and search. It's not an engineering scale-up problem where you know roughly what the end looks like. It's a research problem where you might be wrong about the basic premise.

The other factor was the people. The team is small enough that I know what everyone is working on, and I can argue with any of them over lunch. At a large company, the equivalent conversation requires three layers of scheduling. For the stage of the problem we're at, speed of iteration on ideas matters more than compute budget, as surprising as that sounds.

And I'll be candid, there's a personal element too. At some point you ask yourself whether you want to be one of several hundred very capable people making a large thing slightly better, or one of a few dozen people who might fail completely but might also figure out something fundamental. I'm at a point in my career where the second option is more interesting. If it doesn't work, I'll have learned something real. If it does, I'll have been there when it did.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, the key question was where I could have the most impact on the research direction. Large AI companies have tremendous resources, but resources are only part of the equation. I also care about having the freedom to pursue a question deeply and being able to move quickly from an idea to an experiment.

That was the appeal of RSI: the opportunity to help shape what we work on and how we approach it. Of course, a smaller organization comes with more uncertainty. But I felt that the opportunity to build something made that tradeoff worthwhile.
